query:
title: Go generated model rename

question: Our stable Go SDK has a model named A. I renamed the TypeSpec model to B and added @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "A"), but regeneration still removes the exported Go type A. How can I keep the released Go type name?
ground_truth: Use a Go-scoped client name on the current TypeSpec model: @@clientName(B, "A", "go") in client.tsp. Regenerate and verify the public type remains A. The breaking-change guide explicitly identifies this @renamedFrom pattern as an exported-type rename that invalidates references to A; it prescribes clientName to restore the original name.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: model, enum, and union name changes

query:
title: Go field renamed after TypeSpec update

question: I renamed property a to b in my TypeSpec model Test and added @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "a"). Our released Go struct has A, but regeneration replaces it with B. How do I keep A for Go without changing the other languages?
ground_truth: Apply @@clientName(Test.b, "a", "go") in client.tsp and regenerate. Target the current TypeSpec property Test.b; the Go-scoped name restores the original generated field A. Renaming the exported field otherwise breaks existing field access.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: property name changes

query:
title: Go enum value rename

question: In my TypeSpec enum Test, I renamed member a to b with @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "a"). The wire value hasn't changed, but the generated Go constant name has. How can I retain the old Go name?
ground_truth: Apply @@clientName(Test.b, "a", "go") to the current TypeSpec enum member in client.tsp, then regenerate and check the resulting constant. Renaming an exported enum constant breaks callers referencing the old name even if the wire value stays the same. Target the source enum and member names, accounting for Go naming transformations.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: enum value name changes

query:
title: Go changelog uses a shortened model name

question: My TypeSpec model is WebPubSubSettings, but it appears as Settings in the Go changelog for package webpubsub. Which name should I target in client.tsp when I customize it for Go?
ground_truth: Target WebPubSubSettings, the actual TypeSpec model. The Go emitter trims a matching package-name prefix on a word boundary to avoid stuttering, so the generated Settings name is not the source symbol to customize. Inspect the regenerated Go name after applying the source customization.

expected_references.title: Go naming mechanisms: stuttering cut

query:
title: Preserve a renamed Go Begin method

question: I renamed our TypeSpec LRO from create to provision without changing its long-running behavior. The Go method changed from BeginCreate to BeginProvision. How should I preserve BeginCreate?
ground_truth: Customize the current source operation's bare name: @@clientName(provision, "create", "go"), qualified with its actual namespace or interface in client.tsp. The Go emitter adds Begin, so do not target BeginProvision or put BeginCreate in the override. Regenerate and verify BeginCreate. This addresses a rename, not a switch between synchronous and LRO behavior.

expected_references.title: Go naming mechanisms: list and LRO operation naming
Go breaking changes: operation name changes

query:
title: Set up client.tsp for Go customizations

question: I need Go-scoped client naming overrides. Where should I put client.tsp relative to main.tsp, which file imports which, and do I change the entry point in tspconfig.yaml?
ground_truth: Place client.tsp alongside main.tsp in the service specification directory. client.tsp becomes the client-generation entry point and imports main.tsp plus @azure-tools/typespec-client-generator-core; bring Azure.ClientGenerator.Core and your service namespace into scope. Do not import client.tsp from main.tsp, and do not modify the entry point in tspconfig.yaml. Put the supported Go-scoped customizations in client.tsp.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: client customization entry point and imports

query:
title: Make an acronym-casing fix durable

question: My reviewer found an acronym-casing issue in our generated Go SDK. I changed the .go file, but regeneration discarded my fix. Where should I correct the name?
ground_truth: Make the customization in the TypeSpec project's client.tsp, then regenerate the SDK and send the corrected output back for review. For a naming override, use the supported Go-scoped clientName customization on the actual source symbol. Do not edit generated Go output as the durable fix: regeneration overwrites it.

expected_references.title: Generate a Go SDK: TypeSpec customization and regeneration
Go breaking changes: client customizations

query:
title: Go exported property type change

question: I used @typeChangedFrom to change a response property from string to int32. Our generated Go field now changes from *string to *int32. Can I fix that compatibility issue with a clientName customization?
ground_truth: No. The public field type change requires callers to change conversions or value handling. The Go breaking-change guide identifies this @typeChangedFrom pattern as breaking and says it cannot be resolved through client customizations. Restoring a name does not restore the old field type.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: property type changes

query:
title: Removed operation disappears from Go

question: I removed an operation from our new API version with @removed. Regeneration deletes the Go method our callers use. Can a client naming override recover the method?
ground_truth: No. Removing the operation removes the client method and breaks callers that invoke it. The Go guide lists operation deletion as a breaking change that cannot be resolved through client customizations. This is different from renaming an operation that still exists.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: operation deletion

query:
title: Added required Go operation parameter

question: My Go method used to take ctx, resourceName, and options. I added a required region parameter in the specification, and generation puts it before options. Why is this additive service feature source-breaking?
ground_truth: Existing calls do not supply the newly required argument, so they no longer match the method signature. The Go guide identifies required parameter addition as breaking and says it cannot be resolved through client customizations. An additive service capability is not necessarily an additive Go API change.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: required parameter addition

query:
title: Keep a synchronous method after an LRO change

question: I changed our service operation to a long-running template. The Go SDK now exposes BeginCreate and a poller instead of Create and its direct result. Can I just rename BeginCreate back to Create to preserve compatibility?
ground_truth: No. Switching to an LRO changes both the generated method name and its return shape, from a direct result to a poller. The Begin prefix is applied automatically. The Go guide classifies switching between synchronous and LRO forms as breaking and not resolvable through client customizations; a name alone cannot restore the old contract.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: long-running operation changes

query:
title: Inherently fixed protocol values

question: I'm modeling an Azure API value that can only be IPv4 or IPv6. Is there any exception to the TypeSpec no-enum guidance, or must I always include string as an extensible variant?
ground_truth: The rule permits suppression when the set is inherently immutable, with IPv4 versus IPv6 as its example. For sets that can grow, use an open union containing the base scalar. A small set today is not enough by itself to justify treating it as immutable; versioning enums are also explicitly allowed.

expected_references.title: Azure core no-enum rule: suppression and versioning exceptions

query:
title: Keep the released Go operation name

question: I renamed our TypeSpec operation from updateTags to update without changing its PATCH URI or method. My released Go SDK loses UpdateTags. Is that a client breaking change, and how can I retain the old Go name?
ground_truth: Yes. Removing UpdateTags breaks existing Go callers even when the HTTP method and URI stay the same. In client.tsp, apply a Go-scoped name to the current TypeSpec operation, for example @@clientName(update, "updateTags", "go"), qualified with its actual namespace or interface. Regenerate and confirm that UpdateTags is retained. Target the TypeSpec operation, not the generated Go method.

expected_references.title: Go breaking changes: operation name changes

query:
title: Model SKU values that can grow

question: I'm defining our Azure API's SKU as enum Sku { Small, Large }, but we expect more string values later. What TypeSpec shape should I use instead?
ground_truth: Use an extensible union, for example union Sku { Small: "Small", Large: "Large", string }. The base string variant permits future values. Azure core's no-enum guidance explains that TypeSpec enums are closed and adding values in later API versions is breaking. Enums remain allowed for versioning; suppress the rule only for inherently immutable value sets.

expected_references.title: Azure core no-enum rule and suppression guidance

query:
title: Two breaking-change gates on my ARM specification

question: My specification change targets public main and has both BreakingChangeReviewRequired and BreakingChange-Go-Sdk labels. ARM review is also pending, and we have no branch-specific waiver. In what order should I complete these reviews and request merge?
ground_truth: First resolve the specification-level breaking-change review represented by BreakingChangeReviewRequired. Next complete ARM review and obtain ARM signoff. Then complete the Go SDK breaking-change review represented by BreakingChange-Go-Sdk, which follows the first two stages. Finally obtain PR approval and satisfy the merge requirements. Do not combine the REST specification and Go SDK gates or put all breaking-change approvals before ARM review.

expected_references.title: Standard specification PR review workflow
Specification-level breaking-change review requirements

query:
title: Is my SDK release PR ready for owner review?

question: I'm preparing a Go SDK PR for release review, not a specification PR. An earlier workflow run was green, but the latest current-commit run failed changelog validation. Copilot has an unresolved inline suggestion about a missing retry-behavior changelog entry, explicitly marked non-blocking. In the normal PR discussion, the reviewer asks me to confirm which API version we intend to ship. The linked specification is approved, but the release plan is blocked on unfinished package-version metadata. There are no new API breaking changes. What needs resolving before approval?
ground_truth: Not ready yet. Fix the current changelog-validation failure, answer the reviewer's API-version question in the PR discussion, and complete the release-plan package-version metadata. Then rerun the affected check and request review. Copilot's inline changelog suggestion is non-blocking, although addressing it alongside the validation fix is sensible. The older green run and approved specification do not clear these outstanding issues; no new ARM or specification breaking-change approval is called for by this SDK-only review.

query:
title: Request Go suppression approval after prerequisites

question: My ARM specification PR targets public main. The latest Next Steps to Merge confirms that REST specification breaking-change approval and ARM signoff are complete. The Go SDK report removes WidgetsClient.GetLegacy because the service no longer implements that operation; a naming override cannot restore it. I've committed the matching entry in sdk-suppressions.yaml, and automation added BreakingChange-Go-Sdk-Suppression, but BreakingChange-Go-Sdk-Suppression-Approved is absent. Several business days have passed without reviewer feedback. What is still pending, and how should I briefly ask the Go owner for help?
ground_truth: The Go suppression still needs reviewer approval; the existing label only confirms the suppression was recognized. You can ask: '@tadelesh, REST breaking-change approval and ARM signoff are complete. Removing WidgetsClient.GetLegacy breaks existing callers, and the service no longer supports it. The matching sdk-suppressions.yaml entry is present; could you review the Go suppression?' Approval remains with the reviewer and applies to this change, not unrelated changes or validation failures.

expected_references.title: SDK breaking changes: suppression recognition and reviewer approval
SDK breaking-change review prerequisites and Go reviewer

query:
title: Regenerate Go from my local TypeSpec edits

question: I'm testing a naming customization in a local azure-rest-api-specs checkout before publishing the specification change. How can I regenerate my existing Go module from those local sources?
ground_truth: From the Go module directory, run tsp-client update --local-spec-repo <path-to-local-spec-repo>. The generation guide documents this local TypeSpec workflow. Keep the customization in the TypeSpec project's client.tsp and regenerate; do not patch the generated Go files as the persistent solution.

expected_references.title: Generate a Go SDK: local TypeSpec generation

query:
title: Find the inner Go generation error

question: My Go SDK validation summary only says generation failed. Where can I find the detailed error before deciding whether to change my model?
ground_truth: Open the validation check's Pipeline result link to the Azure DevOps run, select the error entry, and expand the log group immediately above the error-summary group. That is where the SDK Validation guide directs you to inspect detailed generation errors. Use the concrete diagnostic rather than guessing a model fix from the summary.

expected_references.title: SDK Validation: detailed SDK generation errors

query:
title: Get generated SDK validation artifacts

question: My Go SDK validation completed, and I want to inspect the generated artifacts rather than rely only on the status summary. Where do I find them, and are they always present after a failed run?
ground_truth: Open the specification change's Checks tab, select SDK Validation - Go, follow Pipeline result to the Azure DevOps run, and open its artifacts link. The SDK Validation guide warns that a failed check may not have generated artifacts. Inspect the detailed run logs if the expected output is absent; do not assume every failed run has downloadable generated code.

expected_references.title: SDK Validation: downloading generated artifacts
SDK Validation: detailed SDK generation errors

query:
title: Go README link check fails

question: My Go SDK's link-verification check fails after I added a localized documentation link containing en-us. The URL opens in my browser. What should I check first?
ground_truth: Remove the locale code from the documentation link, then verify the resulting link works. The Go engineering-system guide says link verification checks both link validity and removal of locale codes such as en-us. A URL opening successfully does not by itself satisfy that check.

expected_references.title: Go engineering-system checks: link verification

query:
title: Re-run Go validation after a fix

question: I've fixed the issue that blocked my specification's Go SDK validation. How do I request a fresh Go validation run without changing the specification again?
ground_truth: Comment /azp run SDK Validation - Go on the specification change. This reruns the Go validation check; rerunning an SDK Validation check also re-evaluates SDK Validation Status.

expected_references.title: SDK Validation: re-run checks and re-evaluate status
SDK Validation: status re-evaluation

query:
title: New Go module pipeline preparation

question: I've generated a new ARM Go module, but its review asks me to prepare release pipelines. It has only minimal checks so far. Which documented preparation command applies?
ground_truth: Follow the release-preparation request. For a new service with minimal CI checks, the Go management SDK release guideline specifies /azp run prepare-pipelines. Check the new module's pipeline configuration and ensure the pipeline runs as expected; generation alone is not pipeline preparation.

expected_references.title: Go management SDK release guideline: releases new service

query:
title: Internal Go release still needs approval

question: I've merged our Go release-preparation changes and started the internal pipeline. Does the merge remove the need for the release approval step?
ground_truth: No. The documented Go release process runs the internal Azure DevOps pipeline and requires release approval after both live and recorded test pipelines pass. Merging the preparation changes is an earlier step, not a replacement for that release approval.

expected_references.title: Releasing Go packages: release process, steps 2-3

query:
title: Release preparation changed our changelog

question: I ran Prepare-Release.ps1 for our Go module, and it updated the version and CHANGELOG.md. Can I start the release pipeline with those edits only in my local checkout?
ground_truth: No. The Go release process says changes made by eng/common/scripts/Prepare-Release.ps1 must be committed and merged before continuing. Complete those preparation changes first, then run the internal release pipeline.

expected_references.title: Releasing Go packages: release process, step 2

query:
title: Consume a new API version through Go

question: I've added a new management-plane API version to our service specification. Where can I find the Go work needed to turn that into a consumable SDK release?
ground_truth: Follow the management-plane SDK release process rather than stop at the specification change. The public Go management SDK release guideline covers updating an existing resource provider or onboarding a new service, generating code, completing checks and review, and release preparation. The Go generation guide describes the TypeSpec/tsp-client workflow, and the release guide covers publishing and verifying the module version.

expected_references.title: Go management SDK release guideline: release process
Generate a Go SDK: TypeSpec and tsp-client
Releasing Go packages: release process

query:
title: Merged Go SDK PR but release is blocked

question: My Go SDK PR is merged and its checks passed. The release command says Azure SDK Engineering needs to create or repair the package's release-tracking work item/linkage. The PR body already links a release plan. I haven't checked the plan record or the release pipeline run. Does that mean the linkage is broken, and should I link the PR again?
ground_truth: Not enough evidence yet. A plan link and green PR checks do not show whether release tracking is valid or whether a release ran. I need to check the plan's Go package/PR entry and the corresponding release pipeline's trigger, approval, and failure state before recommending a repair. If those records are inaccessible, please share the plan and run links or route the reported blocker to Azure SDK Engineering. Do not relink an already-linked PR or start another release merely on this message; the root cause and required repair are still unverified.

query:
title: Release tooling confirms an internal tracking repair

question: The Go SDK PR is merged and already linked to the correct release plan and package. We inspected the plan and the release readiness result: the package's release-tracking work item is missing, and the tool explicitly says only Azure SDK Engineering can repair it. No publish stage ran. Repeating the release command returns the same error. Can someone help me move this forward?
ground_truth: Azure SDK Engineering needs to repair the missing release-tracking work item before this release can proceed. Handoff: 'Azure SDK Engineering, the merged Go SDK PR is already linked to the correct plan and package, but readiness confirms the package's release-tracking work item is missing and no publish stage ran. Could you repair that tracking record and confirm when readiness can be retried?' Include the PR, plan, package, and failed-run links with that request. After the repair, rerun readiness and continue the release; relinking the same PR or repeating the failed command beforehand will not resolve the confirmed blocker.

query:
title: Plan status is empty but the release run is waiting

question: My Go SDK PR is merged, but the plan's Go release status is empty. I checked the matching release run: tests passed, the publish stage has not started, and the run is waiting for the designated release approver. Should I repair the plan link or start another release?
ground_truth: Neither is indicated by this evidence. The existing release run is waiting for human approval, so ask its designated approver to review the pending approval on that run. Once approved, follow the publish stage and verify the exact module version is available, then check release tracking. An empty plan status alone does not establish broken linkage, and starting another run would not remove the current approval requirement.

expected_references.title: Go release process: tests, release approval, and publication verification

query:
title: Check Go module release readiness

question: I'm preparing our Go SDK for release after API review. Which repository checklist should I use before starting release preparation?
ground_truth: Use the Go release checklist: remove go.mod replace directives, include a LICENSE, document public methods and types, check links and samples, prepare release notes and the changelog, document how to enable logging in the README troubleshooting section, and cover champion scenarios with getting-started guidance. Complete the checklist before the release process.

expected_references.title: Releasing Go packages: release checklist

query:
title: Confirm a Go module release is available

question: I've triggered the release pipeline for our Go module. How do I confirm the intended version is actually available to customers rather than just assume the trigger published it?
ground_truth: Check the release pipeline's publish stage, then run `go get <module>@<version>` for the exact version you intended to ship and check that version on pkg.go.dev. Starting a pipeline does not establish publication. If the version cannot be fetched, investigate the release run before announcing availability; a documentation-indexing delay alone does not prove publication failed.

expected_references.title: Releasing Go packages: publication validation, step 4

query:
title: Add a websocket dependency to a different module

question: I'm adding github.com/coder/websocket to a Go SDK module that is neither azservicebus nor azeventhubs. I saw it allowed for those two modules. Is it part of the repository's general dependency allowance?
ground_truth: No. The standards list github.com/coder/websocket as an additional direct dependency for azservicebus and azeventhubs, not as a general allowance. The general third-party list contains testify, godotenv, OpenTelemetry otel modules, and golang/mock. A package-specific exception does not apply to your different module.

expected_references.title: Go module standards: direct dependencies and module-specific exceptions

query:
title: Retire a module without retracting every version

question: I'm retiring our Go module in favor of a replacement. A teammate suggested retracting all old versions to announce the transition. Should I use retraction or deprecation, and where should the notices go?
ground_truth: Use module deprecation for retirement and migration. Retraction is for problematic module versions, not a synonym for retiring a module. The Go deprecation guide calls for a final patch with a // Deprecated: comment and migration instructions in go.mod, a CHANGELOG.md notice, and a README notice under the title. Put MIGRATION.md in the new module. Do not mass-retract otherwise usable versions merely to announce retirement.

expected_references.title: Deprecating Go modules: overview and deprecation process
Deprecating Go modules: final patch and notices

query:
title: Deprecate a module with a replacement

question: I'm retiring our Go module in favor of a stable replacement. Can I delete its code immediately, or what does the Go deprecation guide require first?
ground_truth: Follow the documented deprecation lifecycle. Create MIGRATION.md in the new module, then publish a final patch of the old module with migration instructions in a // Deprecated: go.mod comment, CHANGELOG.md, and the README notice. Update references and request pkg.go.dev removal after that release; this does not stop go get from accessing the module. The guide puts code deletion after an appropriate deprecation period, at least 12 months, with migration time, usage, and replacement-readiness checks.

expected_references.title: Deprecating Go modules: deprecation process, steps 1-5
